newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 21.

text.p: THE INDEPENDENT BUSINESS WEEKLY

A shake-up of New Zealand's life insurance market is imminent. At least four insurers are lining up to buy NZI Life, and others may be waiting in the wings. The Independent understands initial bids are due in next week. NZI Life's parent, General Accident Asia-Pacific, confirmed it is in discussion with several parties and expects to make a decision next month. Page 1.

Serious Fraud Office director Charles Sturt on Thursday admitted he did not understand the "full scope" of winebox structures allegedly used by the Bank of New Zealand in 1989 to conceal a $1 billion exposure to then major shareholder, Fay Richwhite. That was in spite of a letter written to the SFO on 10 July 1992 -- just three months before the SFO received a full set of winebox documents -- warning Sturt that a series of tansactions for the Fay Richwhite/Capital Markets group had apparently been omitted from a list of the BNZ's large exposure to major customers. Page 1.

Maori owners of reserved lands want a mathematical model to work out compensation for them as well as for lessees. It shouldn't be hard, they are sure. If a model can work out losses that will be incurred by lessees in the future, it can work out losses incurred by them in the past. A mathematical model is a key instrument in legislative proposals to reform some 26,000 hectares of Maori reserved land now bound under a statutory-imposed system of perpetual leases with rents reviewable every 21 years. Page 2.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation threatened to walk away from its Sky Television deal if Television New Zealand went ahead with plans to boost its Sky stake above 25 percent. Allowing TVNZ to go above 25 percent would have given it unacceptable influence over Sky, NewsCorp argued, because, under Sky's shareholders' agreement, parties owning 25 percent or more can veto all management decisions. The veto also covers capital expenditure and shareholder changes. Page 3.

Queensland-based Afro Ostrich Farms, a heavy promoter of ostrich investment schemes in New Zealand, has been asked by the Australian Securities Commission to withdraw its advertising in that country. The ASC said Afro's ads painted an overly-optimistic picture of the security and potential returns of the investment. Page 3.

Labour broadcasting spokesman Marian Hobbs is questioning public-owned TVNZ's right to relinquish part of its news service to the privately-owned National Business Review. NBR's planned Sunday night business show has been coldly received by TVNZ news staff. The Independent understands TVNZ's news and current affairs department has no input into the new programme. Page 4.

A large question-mark still hangs over the ownership of the core assets of beleaguered Maori television station Aotearoa Television Network. Aotearoa agreed to pay $2.4 million late last year to buy the assets of an Auckland-based video production company -- 601 Digital -- from a company owned by Auckland accountant Peter Brannigan -- a key witness in the Winebox inquiry -- and former Aotearoa Television finance director Derek Burns. But the station's lawyers were on Thursday still struggling to determine exactly who owns the assets -- Aotearoa, or Burns and Brannigan. Page 6.

More than two months over its initial deadline, the taxation of life insurance and superannuation taskforce, (TOLIS) chaired by Retirement Commissioner Colin Blair is now to report to the government by mid-March. Its original report deadline was before Christmas. TOLIS, whose members include private sector savings and banking industry representatives, Inland Revenue and Treasury officials, was set to look up the alternatives to the present tax treatment of life insurance and superannuation savings products. Page 6.
THE NATIONAL BUSINESS REVIEW

State servcies commissioner Don Hunn was on Thursday seeking legal advice over whether any action could be taken against Serious Fraud Office director Chas Sturt ahead of the winebox inquiry's report. Hunn's move comes as political pressure builds for an inquiry into whether the nation's top corporate cop misled Parliament through inaccurate statements about his office's investigations into the wine-box affair. Page 1.

The National Business Review Business Centre Online on Friday introduces a major news service to the Internet. An "instant news" section was launched at midnight on Thursday providing centre users with access to every New Zealand story filed by Radio New Zealand's 90 news staff and correspondents. The news is being automatically transferred to the centre every half hour, every day. Next Friday the centre will also introduce a comprehensive sports service, drawing on information from Radio New Zealand, Reuters in New Zealand and worldwide, and Dow Jones Telerate. Page 1.

Aotearoa Television funds were used for New Zealand First political purposes, an Auckland photographer claims. A sworn affidavit by photographer Mark Walsh for the first time links the use of Aotearoa's publicly provided funds with the New Zealand First party. He claims that in late March last year, prospective MP Tukoroirangi Morgan ordered photographs for his New Zealand First campaign election and instructed that the bill be sent to Aotearoa Television. Page 1.

TransTasman biscuit maker Arnott's has discovered the hard way the burden of being a branding icon as it copes with the massive financial and logistical implications of an extortion threat. Police in New South Wales and Queensland are still hunting the man who has threatened to spike the company's biscuits with poison if a murder case is not re-opened. Page 2.

The first time Wellington computer shop owners Janice and Kevin O'Brien realized that some of the computers they sold had fake memory cache chips was when they found Commerce Commission investigators trawling through their supplier's records.
Wondering if it was an isolated incident, the couple, who own PC Help, searched the Internet and were appalled to discover the supply of fake chips was a common international practice. Page 3.

New Zealand exporters to Australia, already battling the unfavourable exchange rate, face a further cut in returns on April 1 when Australian Customs impose new charges for processing imports. Traders say the charges -- estimated to total about $100 a consignment but subject to annual increases -- defy the spirit of CER. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and
Trade says they are within World Trade Organisation rules which require them to approximate the cost of the service provided. Page 5.

Auckland will host a key investment conference next month, bringing together leaders from international finance and investment houses. Organised by equity investment broker Doyle Paterson Brown and Bankers Trust with the help of major New Zealand companies, it will concentrate on the political and investment climate following the formation of the National-New Zealand First Coalition. Page 5.

Television New Zealand is considering reducing the amount of advertising it runs at certain peak viewing times, in line with the Coalition government's policy on broadcasting. TVNZ chief executive Chris Anderson told interviewer Brian Edwards on National Radio last Saturday there were ways of maintaining financial performance and keeping viewers happy at the same time. Page 6.

The head of the Serious Fraud Office, Chas Sturt, has stunned wine-box inquiry lawyers by claiming his department has no right to retain documents leaked to it without authorisation. In what's being seen as a new variation on the Pontius Pilate defence, Sturt told the inquiry the wine box had been stolen and he had no statutory powers to keep it or make copies when he received it in October 1992. This is despite telling Parliament in 1994 that he had copied the wine-box documents using "the office's statutory powers". Page 7.

The U.S. company that pulled out of the deal last year to buy animal genetics firm Ambreed NZ is accusing Ambreed's owner, the Dairy Board, of setting up a barrier to keep out foreign competitors. Wisconsin-based ABS Global is expected to lodge a complaint next week with the American Embassy in Wellington, alleging anti-competitive behaviour by another of the board's subsidiaries, Livestock Improvement Corporation (LIC). Other North American interests are also said to be ready to complain. Page 8.
